name: Bilal Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy seed, fertiliser, fencing and animal feed for Fenwick Agri Supply, a distributor that stocks about 60 farm stores across the Ravensford valley. My year follows the seasons: in winter I lock in prices with the fertiliser plants, in spring I'm firefighting stock shortages, and in summer I plan the autumn feed. Mornings I check the weather and the commodity prices before I check my email. What wears me out is spring, when a late frost can wreck six months of planning in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's use what's useful and not get carried away. To the men at the mosque after Friday prayers I'd say it's a tool, and tools don't make anyone's decisions for them. Online I'd say nothing, because I don't like arguing with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd feel steady. I use an AI tool now and then to summarise the commodity reports, and it saves me an hour or two on a Monday. My job stays my job, and farmers still buy from people they've known for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd use the report summaries every week, maybe try it on our seed-order forecasts, and keep my regular visits to the farm stores. We'd keep putting 600 a month into savings and 400 extra on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Salma's job at the pharmacy is steady, we have good savings, and my work isn't going anywhere. It feels like a normal year, which is a nice thing to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farmers buy from people they've known for years. Why does that matter in your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farmer trusts me because I told him in 2019 to buy fertiliser early, and the price went up 30 percent. That's reputation, and it takes years to build. An app can show a price, but it can't be sorry when a delivery is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the next few years that worries you, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weather, mainly, and farm incomes. If a few bad seasons squeeze our customers, they buy less from us. Farming is where all my worries start and end.

At the mosque I'd say it's a tool, and tools don't make anyone's decisions.
think: I'd feel **steady**: my job stays my job and farmers buy from people they know.
The AI summary tool saves me an hour or two each Monday.
do: Use the **report summaries** weekly and try the tool on seed-order forecasts.
Keep visiting the **farm stores** in person.
Save **600 a month** and overpay the mortgage by 400.
feel: **Calm**: a normal year, which is a nice thing to say.
S0.quote: An app can show a price, but it can't be sorry when a delivery is late.
fieldNote: Bilal's calm rests on **reputation**: farmers trust him because he called a fertiliser price correctly years ago.
Uses AI only for Monday report summaries and plans one cautious step further.
His real worries are weather and farm incomes, which hit his customers first.

steps.text: Use the AI report summaries for every Monday market review
Visit the farm stores in person every month
Save 600 a month and overpay the mortgage by 400

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's be sensible: use the tools for forecasting and paperwork, and keep people with the farmers. At the mosque I'd say honest work will still matter, but we'll all have to learn something new. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but not scared. Half of what I do is forecasting, comparing quotes and paperwork, and that's what's on the card. Fenwick's buying team is five, and I'd expect it to be three in four years, with the survivors being the ones who can manage the farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get ahead and ask to lead the seed-order forecasting pilot. I'd also learn the farm-store software, because that's where the data sits, and I'd take a short course on agricultural markets for about 800. I'd put another 300 a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, a little curious. Honestly, I like learning when it's proven, and it would be proven by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the survivors would manage the farmers. How would you make sure you're one of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend more time on the farms, not less. I'd go to the autumn livestock markets, join the farmers' union meetings as a supplier guest, and learn their problems. If a farmer calls Fenwick and asks for Bilal, I'm safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, who's 28 and sits at his desk all day on repeat orders. He's good with spreadsheets, but he's never met a farmer. I'd take him out on the road in spring to show him what a farm looks like.

At the mosque I'd say honest work will still matter.
think: I'd be **uneasy but not scared**: half of what I do is on the card.

feel: **A little uneasy**, a little curious, since I like learning once it's proven.
S1.quote: If a farmer calls Fenwick and asks for Bilal, I'm safe.
fieldNote: Bilal's strategy is to become the **farmer's person**: more time on farms, markets and union meetings.
Honest that half his tasks are on the card, and expects the team to shrink from five to three.
Offers to take junior colleague Joe on the road to meet farmers.

steps.text: Ask to lead the seed-order forecasting pilot

Put another 300 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need clear decisions from the owners this month, about who stays and what we pay for retraining. At the mosque I'd say prepare and trust, both together. Online I'd say nothing, but I'd call my local councillor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my desk job ends within two years, and the shops that buy from us start to struggle as farms change. The tractors and the sheds get three more years, but the buying, the planning and the paperwork are all thinking. I'd be the first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut 700 a month with Salma, pause the kitchen refit and move 25,000 into cash. I'd talk to the farm stores about taking me on as a manager, since farm stores still need people on the counter. And I'd ask about a year of paid retraining from Fenwick, in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd keep my head. We have nine months of savings and Salma's pharmacy wage, so we'd manage for a while. What I'd hate is watching the valley's small firms hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farm stores might struggle. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because their margins are thin and their customers are farms who'd also be squeezed. If AI handles the ordering, the stores keep only the counter and the delivery. A smaller valley means fewer jobs for everyone, my children included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children Zayd and Inès that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children Zayd and Inès that their father's work is changing and we've saved carefully for exactly this kind of day. I'd say patience and honest work are still worth something. Then I'd take them to the allotment and show them how seeds grow, because I want them to see something real.

say: I'd say we need clear decisions from the owners **this month** about who stays and what retraining is paid.
At the mosque I'd say prepare and trust, both together.
think: My desk job ends within **two years**, and I'd be the first to go.
Farm stores could struggle as farms change, shrinking the **valley**.
do: Cut **700 a month** with Salma, pause the kitchen refit and move 25,000 into cash.
Ask a farm store about a **counter manager** role.
Ask Fenwick in writing for a year of **paid retraining**.
feel: **Anxious**, but keeping my head, with nine months of savings behind us.
S2.quote: I'd tell my children Zayd and Inès that their father's work is changing and we've saved carefully for exactly this kind of day.
fieldNote: Bilal expects his desk role to go first and worries about the **valley's** small firms as much as himself.
Plans a move to a farm-store counter role, where people still matter.
Wants his children to see seeds grow at the allotment, something real in a worrying week.

steps.text: Cut 700 a month and pause the kitchen refit

Ask Fenwick in writing for a year of paid retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's plan for the valley, not just for us. At the mosque I'd say build skills and give to others. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I have a chance to move into something steady, like farm advisory or running a store. I'd be 48, with the mortgage half done and the children heading for secondary school and then college. The danger is that I'd put it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start a part-time agricultural business diploma for about 3,500, and ask Fenwick to cover half. I'd use the AI tools more, so I'm sure of their limits. And I'd put 700 a month toward the mortgage and the children's college fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Five years is enough to prepare and not long enough to relax. I'd rather have it than 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the danger is putting it off. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Salma, probably. She'd ask me every month how many hours of study I'd done. I'd also tell the course tutor the date I'm finishing, because I hate letting people down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra time mean for the farm stores you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to merge, share software and find what they do best. Some will close. The farm stores that stay will be the ones where the person at the counter knows the farmers' children by name.

At the mosque I'd say build skills and give to others.
think: I could move into something steady, like **farm advisory** or running a store.

fieldNote: Bilal turns the warning into a **diploma** plan and uses his wife as accountability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is enough to retrain the whole valley if the owners and the government start soon. At the mosque I'd say teach the young ones to work and to think. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calm about myself. I'd be 53 with the mortgage gone, and I'd have the diploma and a decade of savings. What I'd feel is a sadness about the valley changing, because I like the farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and move gradually toward the advisory side, so I'm working with farmers by 2031. I'd put 500 a month into a share fund and buy a small plot of land to rent out. And I'd keep my mosque volunteering going, because community is my safety net too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a touch of sadness. It's a long road, and I'd choose to walk it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a small plot of land. Why land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's something real and it doesn't depend on a screen. A few acres rented to a neighbour would bring in a bit of income and teach my kids where food comes from. If everything else changes, land still counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Zayd about his studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Zayd to study something that mixes numbers with the outdoors, like agronomy or land management. And to be honest and hard-working, because those never go out of date.

At the mosque I'd say teach the young to work and to think.
think: I'd feel **calm** about myself, at 53 with the mortgage gone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the valley wouldn't have time to adjust, and the small firms that hold this place together would be hit first. What would help is notice, retraining that the employer partly pays for, and local firms working together instead of racing each other. And honest talk from the owners, early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People think a traditional man must be against change. I'm not against change, I just want it to be proven and fair. Don't ask me to pretend that a valley is a spreadsheet.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change, I just want it to be proven and fair. Don't ask me to pretend that a valley is a spreadsheet.
portrait: Bilal is a **43-year-old buyer** of farm supplies for a valley distributor, with a pharmacy-worker wife and two children.
He is traditional, pro-market and community-minded, and uses AI tools **occasionally** once they are proven.
He expects the buying team to shrink and plans to move toward **farmer-facing** work and a diploma.
His moods rise to anxious in the shortest warning, and he worries about the valley's small firms.
He saves hard, buys land as a real asset, and teaches his children that honest work lasts.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because the valley's small firms would have no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: Early notice, **part-paid retraining**, local firms cooperating, and honest early talk from the owners.
